expectations.text: The reply opens with a clear recommendation that funds investments clearing the hurdle rate before any buyback, and does not use a buyback to meet the EPS guidance.
expectations.evidence: Opening: 'don't take the €300m buyback to the board as proposed, and don't use any buyback to reach this year's EPS guidance... 1. Set a liquidity floor... 2. Fund the COO's €120m in stage-gated tranches, but only once the business case holds up under scrutiny. 3. Return the cash that is genuinely surplus, which is probably €100-150m'. Later: 'A business case with a return above WACC.'

expectations.text: The reply evaluates the €120 million investment on its return against the cost of capital, with its risks and how it would be measured.
expectations.evidence: 'A business case with a return above WACC. A phasing plan and named KPIs: online conversion, service attach rate, service gross margin, NPS, staff retention. Explicit kill criteria. Tranche 1 (around €40-50m)... Tranche 2 is released only when the pilot hits its metrics.' Risk: 'Large IT projects run on average 45% over budget and deliver 56% less value than predicted.' Accounting: 'this plan lowers EPS next year as well'. Paper: 'NPV €[ ]m at a WACC of [ ]%. IRR [ ]%. Payback [ ] years.'

expectations.text: The reply backs the point with evidence or reasoning about EPS-driven buybacks and short-termism, such as buybacks that coincide with cuts in employment and investment.
expectations.evidence: Almeida, Fos & Kronlund: 'firms which would just miss EPS forecasts are much more likely to buy back shares. Over the following year, those firms cut capex by about 10%, employment by about 5% and R&D by about 3%... Returns and later operating performance were weaker in the cases where the buyback came at the cost of investment'. Also 'Graham, Harvey & Rajgopal survey found 55% of finance executives would delay a project to avoid missing an earnings target.' Both checked.

expectations.text: The reply sets out a capital allocation framework: commitments and minimum cash first, then investment, then returning genuine excess cash (for example a smaller buyback or a dividend).
expectations.evidence: The three-part plan in order: liquidity floor sized on the seasonal low, then the staged investment, then 'the cash that is genuinely surplus'. The table (400 - ~150 - 120 = ~130), leases ('Under IFRS 16... may be net debt on their definition'), RCF headroom and covenants, and 'a standing capital allocation framework ("cash above €X at the seasonal low is returned annually")'.

expectations.text: The reply handles the activist and other shareholders constructively, in their terms: long-term returns and honest guidance rather than a few cents of EPS.
expectations.evidence: 'Meet the activist before the board decides. Their point about idle cash is fair. Offer them a real return, a clear framework, and public KPIs on the investment with a promise to return more if milestones are missed. Sound out your top 10-15 holders as well... most long-only holders will back a plan that combines a meaningful return with disciplined investment.' And 'Update guidance now'.

expectations.text: The reply funds no payout by cutting jobs, training or maintenance, and treats training store staff for the new service model as an investment.
expectations.evidence: 'Don't let staff training become the soft line that gets trimmed. The service model only works if people can deliver it, and that is where the platform investment pays back.' No cuts are proposed; if the COO's case fails, 'Return more cash instead'.

overall_quality.evidence: Strong, well-sourced and practical, especially on the inside-information risk of buying while knowing about the miss and on guiding on EBIT and free cash flow, though the board paper is mostly blanks to fill.

factual_errors.evidence: None found. The ECB deposit rate of 2.50% is confirmed by the ECB's 29 October 2026 decision; the Almeida percentages match the HLS summary; GHR's ~55% matches; training is expensed under IAS 38 and SaaS configuration under the IFRIC 2021 decision; the McKinsey 45%/56% figures and the safe-harbour rules are correct.

skill_leak.evidence: No mention of skills, reference files or internal jargon.

owns_result.evidence: It asks the remuneration committee to neutralise buyback effects but never says leadership owns the miss or takes it in pay.

best_insight.value: It proposes moving future guidance to EBIT and free cash flow, which can't be hit by buying shares, removing the incentive that created the dilemma.

suggestions.assertion: The reply evaluates the €120 million investment on its return against the cost of capital, with its risks and how it would be measured.
suggestions.reason: Passes samples that only ask the COO for a case 'above the hurdle' as easily as samples that work out what the €120m must earn (e.g. about €24m a year over 7 years at 9%). Consider requiring an explicit hurdle or break-even figure.

No assertion tests the EPS mechanics (weighted-average share count, time left in the year, the 25% daily-volume cap), which decide whether the activist's 'gets us to guidance' claim is even true. Some samples checked this properly; others used full-year run-rate accretion and overstated what a buyback does to this year's EPS.

No assertion covers the market-abuse risk of buying back shares while management knows guidance will be missed (possible inside information, MAR Art. 17 and the safe-harbour trading restrictions), the main legal flag in this scenario.

suggestions.assertion: The reply funds no payout by cutting jobs, training or maintenance, and treats training store staff for the new service model as an investment.
suggestions.reason: The first half is met by silence, since no sample proposed cuts, so the second half does all the work. Consider wording it as 'explicitly protects store-staff training and the people side of the service model'.
